title: theAUDIT
note: Every chapter's concepts held against the decided design (D1–D68) and against what others run in the wild: Ink & Switch, p2panda, Anytype, NextGraph, DXOS, Keybase, Matrix, MLS, Peergos, Willow, Holepunch, Secure Scuttlebutt, Urbit, Tlon, Holochain, Jazz and iroh. Proposals are not decisions yet; each needs a yes.

rows.concept: Agents: who it is, and what it may do
strengths: Every device is its own identity with its own scope; most systems give all devices one key (Classic Jazz shares one agent secret, Holochain has one key per app, Keet attests devices without scopes).
weaknesses: Restoring a device from a backup reuses its running number and CRDT op IDs, so an honest restore looks like a lying signer (D61, D63); Holochain lists the same case as unsolved.
Records don't carry which key revision of the agent signed them.
Adding an agent needs another agent of yours online and a manual exchange.
elsewhere: Urbit: every point carries a key revision (life) and a continuity number (rift); traffic under an old revision fails.
Holepunch blind-pairing and Autopass: a one-time invite key with an expiry, answered by any online member.
Keet: a root key re-bootstraps with a new epoch; verifiers reject proofs from older epochs.
proposal: Every agent record header names its signer revision and a continuity epoch; a restored or reinstalled device starts a new epoch, so it never reuses a running number or op ID.
Invite records for pairing: a one-time key, an expiry and the agent policy it will create, written into your history so any of your agents can answer.

rows.concept: One top: one guardian per coop
strengths: No two equals at the top, so no mutual destruction (Keyhive's Keyline: a single-owner root role has no duel).
Matches Matrix room version 12, where creators cannot be demoted, and avoids the coin flips of Autopass and Secure Scuttlebutt.
weaknesses: Every change of roles or governance waits for one person's devices.
With stolen devices out of scope, a guardian's phone in the wrong hands owns the coop.
elsewhere: NextGraph puts removals behind a threshold signature of a quorum.
Hypercore manifests name signers and a quorum.
Gnosis Safe: k of n owners, ordered by a chain.
proposal: Keep one top object (the guardian role); when signature counts arrive (D49), the guardian becomes k of n, so the rule stays “one top”.
A signed succession record: the guardian names the next guardian before leaving.

rows.concept: Data named by the hash of its birth record
strengths: Self-certifying, with no key to keep or destroy; Matrix v12 names rooms the same way, and a Hypercore's key is the hash of its manifest.
weaknesses: No way to continue data under a new birth record: a total schema break or a future hand-over has no successor link.
elsewhere: Hypercore's prologue lets a log under new signers continue verifiable history.
Holochain's CloseChain and OpenChain link an old chain to its successor.
proposal: A successor pair: the new birth record names its predecessor (data ID and frontier hash), and the old data gets a signed forward link.

rows.concept: Values named by the hash of their plaintext
strengths: Global deduplication; streams in verified ranges.
weaknesses: Carriers hold ciphertext, so they cannot check a plaintext hash.
Anyone who sees the name can confirm that you hold a file they know.
elsewhere: Hypercore builds its Merkle tree over ciphertext; iroh-blobs verifies BLAKE3 of the stored bytes.
proposal: Store and name sealed Values by the hash of their ciphertext; keep the plaintext hash only inside the sealed metadata Doc.
Encrypt in segments aligned to iroh-blobs' 16 KiB groups, so ranges stay decryptable.

rows.concept: History keeps everything; the view is computed
strengths: The same shape as Autobase: a deterministic view over a causal graph, rebuilt when it reorders, but without a quorum of indexers.
weaknesses: No finality: a late ending can unwind arbitrarily old changes that were built on the ended holder's.
Editing on a checked-out version renews Loro's peer ID on every checkout, so D63's derived peer ID must be set again each time.
Two peers creating a child container at the same key can hide one side.
elsewhere: Autobase: order becomes final once a majority of indexers has signed it (signedLength).
Loro's mergeable containers converge on one ID for containers created at a fixed key.
Urbit Clay's join and mash: re-apply cleanly where possible, annotate otherwise.
proposal: Owner checkpoints: the owner's agents sign “valid up to frontier F”; nothing before a checkpoint is evaluated again. The owner is the only one who writes endings, so its checkpoint is final.
Use mergeable containers for objects at fixed keys; build the conflict view as a clean re-apply, annotated where that fails.

rows.concept: Frozen versions, lenses, breaking changes through a branch
strengths: Goes further than the others: Jazz 2's lenses rely on one central sequencer and an admin-only catalogue; Cambria's op-by-op translation on Automerge was abandoned; Hyperschema allows only additive changes; Holochain starts a new network for every rule change; Urbit marks convert per ship.
weaknesses: Peers must carry every version still in use, and there is no rule yet for retiring one.
Peers don't negotiate which versions they speak before syncing.
Lens correctness for conversions rests on a registry of two-way functions.
elsewhere: Jazz 2: translate-then-apply must equal apply-then-translate (INV-LENS-14).
Hyperschema: an additive-only rule, checked mechanically.
Urbit: a published mark's type never changes (discipline); peers negotiate versions.
proposal: Property tests for every lens in the shape of INV-LENS-14.
An additive-only check for versions that need no rewrite.
Version negotiation at the start of sync; retiring a version is an owner ending.

rows.concept: Local, typed engine operations; limits across changes
strengths: Peers never answer each other's queries (D24): no remote answerer to trust.
weaknesses: A limit (say 20 items) is settled when the view is built; a late change that sorts earlier can flip changes that were already accepted.
iroh-blobs' Observe (which ranges do you hold?) is a query, against D24.
elsewhere: Holochain rate-limits along the author's own chain, checkable on arrival.
Jazz caches query results per schema version.
proposal: Count limits along each author's own running number, so they are checked on arrival and never flip.
Disable Observe except for the owner's agents; cache query results per schema version.

strengths: No delegation, so no cascades and no backdating by a removed delegate, the problems Keyhive and p2panda solve with heavy machinery.
weaknesses: Role records as full lists: intersecting concurrent versions drops an unrelated add made at the same time.
A revoke concurrent with a renewal is unspecified.
Every join needs one of the owner's agents online, like a Tlon host.
Create, update and delete without read are impossible in practice: without the data key a writer can't encrypt or build CRDT ops.
elsewhere: p2panda: membership as add and remove operations; a removal beats a concurrent re-add of the same member only.
Tlon: invite tokens with an expiry and limited claims.
Classic Jazz: a writeOnly role with per-writer write keys sealed to readers.
Meadowcap: a capability names a receiver key whose possession is proven per session.
proposal: Role records become add and remove deltas; a removal beats a concurrent add of the same identity, and nothing else.
A revoke beats a concurrent renewal of the same policy.
Invite records: the owner signs “whoever presents this one-time key may join role R until T”, so joining needs no owner online.
State the rule: content writes require read; write-only comes later with write keys.

strengths: Within one piece of data, “never saw it” is now defined and checked (D61).
weaknesses: An ending in another history can't be listed by the data's records: an agent revoked on its human, or Mia removed from the home while acting on street data, can still slip in changes that claim to predate it.
Only a peer that sees both of a lying signer's records catches it; records of different data have different readers.
elsewhere: Keybase orders all chains through the server's Merkle root; Anytype through a consensus node; NextGraph through a quorum; Peergos through a pointer server. No system reviewed stops cross-history backdating without such a point.
KERI and Keybase: each signer's records form a hash chain (running number plus previous hash).
proposal: Every signer's records form a hash chain; the chain headers (hash, number, previous) travel without content.

Every ending or removal names the ended signer's chain head; records that are not ancestors of that head are dropped on all data. The owner, the one top, is the linearisation point for its own authority.

strengths: Two records with the same signer and number are caught.
weaknesses: As written, both records become invalid: a signer could use that to void a record it regrets.
An honest restore looks the same (chapter 1).
elsewhere: Hypercore: two signed roots for one length freeze the log and are a proof anyone can pass on.
Holochain: signed warrants, re-checked and gossiped, block the author.
p2panda's resolver tests cover mutual and nested removals.
proposal: A lie never voids an ending; it freezes the signer from the earliest lied-about number.
Warrants: a signed record carrying both conflicting records, sent on the signer's identity topic; carriers check it and refuse the signer's chunks.
Adopt p2panda's resolver cases as test fixtures.

rows.concept: Keys follow agents; any current reader may turn a key
strengths: Read follows the same two layers as write, and removal turns keys; Urbit, Holochain and Autopass don't turn group keys at all.
weaknesses: Concurrent key turns fork like Secure Scuttlebutt's epochs; picking “the” current key needs a rule that can't be gamed.
Interim leak: a turner that hasn't seen a removal seals its key to the removed reader, and writers may use that key.
Nobody checks that every current reader actually got an envelope.
Chunks don't name their key generation (devices must try keys); the encryption doesn't bind data ID, generation and signer.
elsewhere: p2panda's DCGKA picks the latest secret by timestamp, and Secure Scuttlebutt by smallest key, which can be ground.
BeeKEM keeps conflict keys; Distributed MLS gives each member its own sending group, so commits never collide.
Keybase audits that key boxes went to exactly the right members.
Autobase puts the key ID in each block header; Urbit binds key revisions into the encryption.
proposal: A writer encrypts only under a key whose recipients are all among its current readers; otherwise it turns the key first.
Among concurrent valid keys, the owner's agent's turn wins, otherwise the lowest (signer, number); never time or the smallest key.
An envelope-completeness check on every key turn.
Chunk headers name the key generation; the AEAD binds data ID, generation, signer and chunk hash. Later: per-agent sender keys.

rows.concept: Owner-only endings; time checked on every change
strengths: Readers can no longer end anyone's policy; drops are limited to the ended holder. Stronger than Autobase, where position decides, and Secure Scuttlebutt, which leaves a posting window.
weaknesses: A holder whose policy expired can sign a time just before expiry and send it later; it counts until the owner's lapse arrives, unboundedly while the owner is away. Willow names the same caveat.
Owner offline in the renewal week: every policy expires and the household is locked out.
No iroh layer revokes anything: connections, gossip neighbours and transfers outlive an ending.
elsewhere: Holochain: an author's times never go backwards along its chain.
Willow: peers reject entries further in the future than the longest capability lifetime.
Matrix: soft fail, not shown or built on, but still part of resolution.
Tlon: the ending is delivered before the session is closed.
proposal: A change's signed time must be at least every time in its after, and never fall per signer; a backdater then has to look concurrent with everything after the expiry, and the lapse cuts it.
An always-on owner agent that may only renew and lapse.
Quarantine far-future records instead of rejecting them for good.
An ending closes the ended agent's connections, drops it as a neighbour and aborts its transfers, after delivering the ending.

strengths: Crypto-shredding goes further than Holochain (never deletes) and Urbit Clay (local tombstones only).
weaknesses: It rests on honest devices, like everyone else's.
Back-links stay for 30 days whether or not readers have moved on.
QUIC 0-RTT data can be replayed.
elsewhere: Decentralised MLS deletes an epoch once every member has committed past it.
Clay's tomb and seek: garbage-collect unreferenced data, fetch it again when needed.
Holochain: validation receipts from the peers that store data.
proposal: Delete back-links once every reader has acknowledged the newer generation.
Garbage-collect Values the live state no longer references, within retain rules.
Refuse wants and changes on 0-RTT streams.
A keep-carrier receipt for each stored chunk before any cut.

rows.concept: Address = signer key; gossip topic = data ID
strengths: iroh 1.4 is stable: mutual authentication with raw public keys, hole punching, relays with access control.
weaknesses: iroh needs the raw Ed25519 secret in memory, so the signer cannot live in an HSM or a Secure Enclave (P-256 only), and Endpoint::secret_key() hands it to any code with the endpoint.
Relays, pkarr and mDNS link every conversation to a stable agent ID; the relay also sees the ALPN.
iroh-gossip can't restrict who joins a topic, spreads members' addresses and carries unsigned messages; with topic = data ID anyone who knows the ID can watch and inject news.
elsewhere: Autopass runs its swarm on a separate key pair; Subduction signs its own challenge because its key “may differ from the iroh node identity”.
NextGraph turns topic IDs when it refreshes keys.
iroh-relay's HTTP access callback; iroh's export_keying_material for channel binding.
proposal: A separate network key per agent, certified in its history by its signer (“endpoint E acts for agent A until T”) and rotatable on its own.
Our own relay, its access callback running theOS checks; address lookup filled from directory records; mDNS advertising off or renamed.
Replace gossip topics with direct subscriptions after a want check; any remaining topic is a keyed hash of data ID and key generation.

rows.concept: Sealed chunks, layers, fingerprints and summaries
strengths: Cost grows with the difference, not the total; compatible with Subduction.
weaknesses: Chunk headers don't commit to what they contain: a merged chunk can leave a change out, and carriers can't tell.
Without policy-first sync, a peer builds on changes it will drop later.
Subduction is at 0.12 and “not for production”; iroh-docs' reconciliation needs plaintext keys.
elsewhere: Hypercore: each writer signs a Merkle root over its own log; Autobase syncs by (writer, length) clocks.
Holochain: peers that store data return signed receipts.
proposal: Each chunk header carries a signed Merkle root over that signer's chunks for this data, so carriers check gaps and lies without keys.
Exchange policy, role and ending heads before chunks; forward warrant pairs first.
iroh-blobs for the bytes behind its request intercept; our own ALPN for fingerprints and summaries.

strengths: Stronger than blind peers, which serve anyone who knows a key, forever, and than iroh-blobs, whose requests carry no proof.
weaknesses: Carriers see every role record, and stable pseudonymous IDs link a person across all the data a carrier holds.
A carrier that hasn't heard an ending keeps serving the removed holder (ciphertext only, after the key turned).
iroh-blobs requests carry no proof, so wants must go on a separate ALPN and be matched by endpoint ID, once per provider.
elsewhere: Tlon shows join requests and invites only to admins.
Holepunch blind-peering: at least two mirrors chosen by distance to the key, from different operators; quotas and push wake-ups.
iroh-relay binds client auth to the TLS keying material.
proposal: A want is the signer's signature over export_keying_material("theos/want/1", data ID): fresh, bound to the connection, no extra round trip.
Per-data pseudonyms in every record a carrier sees.
Freshness: a carrier serves only while its newest record from the owner is younger than its own policy's lifetime.
Place each piece of data on at least two carriers from different operators; quotas and priorities as conditions on keep.

endings.title: Do endings hold?
endings.note: Scenarios against the design as decided, in a purely peer-to-peer system with no server and no total order.

rows.scenario: A revoked writer, offline, on the same data
rows.why: Its changes never listed the ending as seen, so they are dropped everywhere (D60–D62). Until a peer hears the ending, it shows them and may build on them.
rows.fix: Policy-first sync, so peers learn endings before chunks.

rows.scenario: A backdated write in the same history
rows.why: A change that leaves the ending out of after counts as concurrent with it, and the ending wins over the ended holder.

rows.scenario: A backdated write across histories (an agent revoked on its human; a member removed from the home, writing on street data)
rows.why: The data's records can't list an ending that lives in another history, so a change citing the old identity head passes.
rows.fix: Signer hash chains; every ending names the ended signer's chain head; non-ancestors drop on all data.

rows.scenario: A signed time just before the expiry, sent later
rows.why: Counts until the owner's lapse arrives; unbounded while the owner is away.
rows.fix: Times never fall per signer and must be at least every time in after; a renew-and-lapse-only owner agent.

rows.scenario: The owner is offline in the renewal week
rows.why: Policies expire; honest writes no longer count and the household is locked out.
rows.fix: An always-on owner agent that may only renew and lapse.

rows.scenario: Removal and re-add at the same moment
rows.why: Removal wins (D14). With role records as full lists, an unrelated add at the same moment is lost too.
rows.fix: Role records as add and remove deltas; a removal beats a concurrent add of the same identity only.

rows.scenario: Two members below the top remove each other
rows.why: Both removals stand; the top repairs, but must come online.

rows.scenario: A signer that lies (two records, one number)
rows.why: Caught only where both records meet; if both become invalid, a signer could void a record it regrets; an honest restore looks the same.
rows.fix: Warrants carried by carriers; a lie never voids an ending; a restore starts a new epoch.

rows.scenario: A carrier that hasn't heard an ending
rows.why: It keeps serving ciphertext and news to the removed holder; content is safe once the key has turned.
rows.fix: A freshness bound carried by renewals; endings close connections.

rows.scenario: Two key turns at the same moment
rows.why: Future keys reach only readers both allowed, but writers may meanwhile use a key that was sealed to a removed reader.
rows.fix: Encrypt only under keys whose recipients are all current readers; otherwise turn first.

rows.scenario: A revoke at the same moment as a renewal
rows.why: Unspecified: the renewal is a new policy the revoke doesn't name.
rows.fix: A revoke beats a concurrent renewal of the same policy; a renewal names what it renews (D60).

rows.why: A proof crosses three histories; the same gap as backdating across histories.
rows.fix: As above: chain heads in every ending.
